title: The Wicked Man's Portion: Zophar's Second Speech
summary: Zophar, stung by what he hears as an insult, answers Job with a single long portrait of the wicked man. His success is brief, his wealth is swallowed only to be vomited up, and God's anger rains down on him while he is still eating. Zophar ends by calling this the portion and inheritance God has appointed for the wicked.
story: We are in the second cycle of speeches between Job and his three friends (chapters 15 to 21). In chapter 19 Job begged his friends for pity and then reached for the astonishing confidence that his Redeemer lives and that he would see God. He also warned them that their persecution of him would bring judgment on them. Zophar hears only the warning. He answers not the hope of chapter 19 but the threat, and he does so by restating the one thing the friends keep saying: the wicked always come to ruin, and quickly. This is Zophar's last speech in the book. In the third cycle Eliphaz and Bildad speak, but Zophar is never given a third turn, and the friends' voice runs out. Job's reply in chapter 21 will take Zophar's picture apart piece by piece.
historical:
Like the rest of the dialogue, the chapter is set in an undated patriarchal world in the land of Uz, somewhere east of Israel, and the book's own date of composition is debated (the introduction sets out the positions). What stands behind this chapter is less a historical event than a widely held belief. Across the ancient Near East, wisdom writers taught that the world has a moral order: the gods, or in Israel the LORD, reward the upright and bring the wicked down. Egyptian instruction texts and Mesopotamian proverb collections share the conviction, and so do many of Israel's own proverbs and psalms.

Zophar appeals to that tradition as ancient and universal: it has been so since man was placed on the earth (verse 4). He is not inventing a doctrine. He is defending the consensus of his world, and he assumes that anyone who questions it has abandoned wisdom itself.
cultural:
Zophar's imagery comes from daily life in a land where wealth meant food, flocks, and houses. The wicked man savors evil the way a person keeps a sweet morsel under the tongue (verses 12-13), but it turns in his stomach into the venom of cobras. Ancient people commonly believed that snake venom came from the gall or bile, and the Hebrew word for gall in verse 14 is linked with bitterness and poison. The rivers of honey and cream in verse 17 are a proverbial picture of plenty, close to Israel's own description of the promised land as flowing with milk and honey.

Verse 19 names the crime behind the picture: he has oppressed and forsaken the poor and seized houses he did not build. In a society without banks or police, a powerful man could foreclose on debtors and take their homes, and the prophets and wisdom writers repeatedly condemn it. Verse 10 imagines a reversal in which his sons must court the favor of the poor, and his own hands give back what he took. The weapons of verse 24, an iron weapon and a bronze-tipped arrow, reflect the warfare of the Iron Age, when both metals were in use.
literary: Almost the whole speech is a single extended portrait, a genre common in wisdom literature, where a type of person (the fool, the sluggard, the wicked) is described from rise to fall. Zophar opens with a brief personal preface (verses 2-3), states his thesis (verses 4-5), and then develops it through images that keep returning to eating: sweetness in the mouth, food that sours in the stomach, wealth swallowed and vomited, an appetite never satisfied, and finally God's fury rained down on the man as he eats (verse 23). The chapter closes with a summary line in the style of a wisdom teacher's verdict, “This is the wicked man’s portion from God” (verse 29), which echoes the closing formula of Bildad's portrait in 18:21. Notice what is missing: Zophar never addresses Job directly after the opening, and he never mentions the possibility of repentance. The door he left open in chapter 11 has closed.

outline.t: The triumph of the wicked is brief
Evil tastes sweet and turns to poison
God's fury overtakes the greedy man
The wicked man's portion from God

doctrines.note: Zophar is right that God judges wickedness and that ill-gotten wealth does not finally satisfy. His error is in timing and application: he insists that judgment always falls swiftly and visibly in this life, and he uses the principle to convict a man God himself called blameless (1:8).

The chapter shows how true wisdom can be misused. Much of Zophar's portrait could sit comfortably in Proverbs, yet God will later say that the friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7). Wisdom includes knowing when a true saying does not fit the case.
Zophar reads suffering as a sign of hidden sin. The book as a whole refuses to let that equation stand, and Job's reply in the next chapter attacks it directly.

words.note: Cheleq, portion or share. It is used of a share of plunder, of land, or of one's lot in life. In the Psalms the faithful can say that the LORD himself is their portion. Zophar uses it for the lot God assigns to the wicked (verse 29): disaster is what they have coming.

Nachalah, inheritance. Usually it names the land passed down in a family or allotted to the tribes of Israel, something meant to be held and enjoyed across generations. Paired with portion in verse 29, it turns bitter: the only inheritance the wicked man leaves is ruin.

Bala, to swallow up or engulf. It is the verb behind the chapter's eating imagery in verse 15: he swallows wealth but vomits it out. The same verb is used elsewhere of the earth swallowing Korah and his followers and of a great fish swallowing Jonah.

Chaneph, godless or profane. The word describes someone who has turned away from God, often with the sense of a person whose piety is hollow. Zophar sets it beside the wicked in verse 5, and by implication he places Job in that company.

christ: Zophar's portrait assumes that anyone struck down by God must be wicked. The New Testament tells the story of a righteous man whom onlookers judged in exactly that way. The Gospels describe passers-by mocking Jesus on the cross as one God had abandoned, and Isaiah 53, which the early church read as a portrait of Christ, describes a servant whom people considered stricken by God when in fact he was bearing the sins of others. The link with Job 20 is thematic, not predictive. Zophar's theology has no room for a righteous sufferer, and the gospel is built on one. At the same time, Jesus did not deny what is true in Zophar's warning: his parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21) makes the same point that hoarded wealth cannot secure a life, though it places the reckoning in God's time rather than in visible, immediate disaster.

hard.q: Much of what Zophar says sounds like the Bible's own teaching. Why is he wrong?
hard.a: The difficulty is real. Psalms such as 37 and 73, and many proverbs, also say that the wicked are brief and that God brings them down, and prophets condemn the same oppression of the poor that Zophar names in verse 19. Readers have answered in several ways. One response is that Zophar's error lies in his certainty about timing: he claims the collapse is always swift and visible, which Job and much of Scripture deny (Psalm 73 itself begins with the prosperity of the wicked). Another is that the error is one of application: a general truth about how God governs the world is turned into a diagnosis of a particular sufferer, and in Job's case the diagnosis is false. A third observes that Zophar speaks without compassion and without listening, so that even true words become a weapon. These answers work together. The book's verdict comes in 42:7, where God says the friends have not spoken rightly about him as Job has. Part of what the book teaches is that orthodox sentences can still misrepresent God when they are used to crush a person he has not condemned.

questions: Zophar answers Job's threat but ignores his hope in chapter 19. When have you heard only the part of someone's words that offended you?
What is true in Zophar's picture of greed that never satisfies, and where have you seen it in yourself or in the world around you?
Zophar uses sound teaching to condemn a man God called blameless. How can a person tell whether a true principle actually fits the situation in front of them?
